before:
Whenever your little one shows up looking for their parent, even if they don't know that's what they are doing, you go back to being the one they can rely on, and you're kind to them while you do it. If they show up to have some innocent fun, don't "put them in their place" as the adult. But sometimes they show up as the one who doesn't want to go to bed. Now you're in my mom's place: you still go to bed, and staying kind about it shows them bedtime isn't a lack of love.

(That was the end of the previous section. This paragraph is the first one under the new heading:)

Give the Vow a Physical Reminder
after: (Not written yet. The next paragraph: pair the object with one ordinary promise, like a stuffed animal sitting next to a note that says "When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time." Don't say any of that here.)
brief:
- first paragraph of the section; the heading has just said "Give the Vow a Physical Reminder"
- the guide: "You can give the promise a physical place in the room: a childhood toy, familiar stuffed animal, visible self-love note, or another object that feels steady and kind." Keep the guide's examples (a toy from when you were little, a stuffed animal you've had for a long time, a note to yourself where you'll see it) and "steady and kind".
- the guide: "Choose what it means while you're sober and regulated." Decide what it stands for while you're calm (the article's word: "the last time you were calm", "wait until you're calm and actually ready") and sober.
- the guide: "Let it remind you of the Nurturer or Protector you're practicing becoming." The article already named them: "the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide."
- the guide: "It doesn't speak for the child, contain secret wisdom, or become an oracle. Your adult judgment stays in charge." In plain words: the object isn't your little one talking, it doesn't know anything you don't, and it isn't something you ask what to do; you still decide.
- Don't explain why, and don't end on a line that sums it up.

A first round failed, so this one has to be built differently:
- Three drafts went through the guide's points in the guide's order, one sentence each: the list of objects, decide what it means while calm and sober, the Nurturer or Protector, then the cautions (it isn't your little one talking, it doesn't know anything you don't, you still decide). Two of them were checked, and the AI detector flagged every sentence of both. Don't follow that order, and don't give each point a sentence of its own.
- A cold reader said "it isn't your little one talking" answered a worry nobody had raised. Say what the object is for instead (a reminder you, the grown-up, set up for yourself), and carry the guide's limits in a clause: it doesn't know anything you don't, and you're still the one who decides.
- The cold reader also didn't recognize "the Nurturer or Protector". The article introduced them near its start ("the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide"), so a few words can point back.
- Write it the way the author talks out loud: a sentence can react to the one before it (notice something about it, or push back on it), the way the paragraphs that passed did. No invented facts about the author's life or things he owned, and no joke that lands at the end.
length: three to five sentences, 45 to 85 words
guide_passage: You can give the promise a physical place in the room: a childhood toy, familiar stuffed animal, visible self-love note, or another object that feels steady and kind. Choose what it means while you’re sober and regulated. Let it remind you of the Nurturer or Protector you’re practicing becoming. It doesn’t speak for the child, contain secret wisdom, or become an oracle. Your adult judgment stays in charge.
next: Pair the object with one ordinary promise. A stuffed animal might sit beside a note saying, “When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time.” Symbolic comfort becomes more believable when the Protector follows through.

Joel's standing rules: never call the inner child "the kid"; invent no facts about his life; banned: "doesn't get to decide" and its family, "Fine,"/"Good,"/"Great," as a clause, wry humor. No emojis from the writers.

Acts can be practiced before they feel natural; love is felt. Never word a condition as a question of the reader's sincerity.

cut: bedtime isn't a lack of love.
